scenario: AITA got refusing to back up for someone who drove the wrong way up to an ATM? | My bank has kind of an odd set up for their ATM out front. It’s in a small cut out with clearly marked arrows pointing to which way the entrance is, in addition to the fact that since this is a drive up ATM it makes sense for the machine to be on the left side where the driver would be sitting. That said, it’s very easy for people to turn I to the outcropping the wrong way. This happened today while I went to get some cash. I arrived at my bank and as I took the turn to go into the ATM cut out, another car whipped into it going the wrong way so that their passenger could use the ATM. I was annoyed at this as I was just about to pull up to it and I was in kind of a hurry, since I needed to get to class. She took 15 minutes to do her transactions. She went through at least 3 cards inserting and reinserting the cards at least 2 times each. I sat patiently, yet annoyed, and waited for her to finish. But when she was done was reaching my limit of patience, she then leant out the window of her car and yell at me to move, I didn’t respond, no one was waiting behind me, I had already been late to class, so being more late wouldn’t kill me. I didn’t move. After about 5 minutes of her shouting at me to move, she backed up did a K-turn and left. I told my friend about this when I eventually arrived at class and he told me that I was being a dick for not just backing up since there was no one behind me. However I stick to the notion that I was in the right for not moving because they were going against traffic. AITA?

Clean & Prepare the House (Most Critical First!)** - **Deep clean** high-traffic areas (living room, kitchen, guest rooms). - **Declutter** surfaces, floors, and entryways for a welcoming vibe. - **Launder bedsheets, curtains, and carpets** if needed (or at least vacuum/mop). - **Replace air filters** (if AC/heaters are running) for fresh air. ### **2. Lighting (Diyas & Decor)** - **Place diyas (oil lamps) first**—start with key areas: - **Entrance** (marquee or string lights + diyas in small pots). - **Living room** (center table, shelves, or windowsills). - **Kitchen** (if open to guests) and **puja room** (if applicable). - **Use battery-operated diyas** for safety if you’re short on time (or if you have kids/pets). - **Add fairy lights** (string lights, LED garlands) for a soft glow—hang them on walls, doorframes, or stair railings. ### **3. Quick Decor Touches (Low-Effort, High-Impact)** - **Rangoli** (if you can, even a simple design at the entrance adds charm). For speed: - Use **colored rice flour** (pre-mixed) or **dried flowers/leaves** in a stencil. - Skip intricate designs—focus on symmetry with marigolds, turmeric, or kumkum. - **Mango leaves** (hang or place on walls/doors for auspiciousness). - **Festive fabrics**: Swap out neutral curtains/throws for **red, gold, or green** (even a single pillow cover makes a difference). - **Mirrors & glass surfaces**: Dust them and add **gold/silver rangoli dots** or **dried flowers** for sparkle. ### **4. Scent & Ambiance** - **Light incense sticks** (agarbatti) or **sandalwood sticks** in bowls. - **Simmer pots** (boil cinnamon, cardamom, cloves, and orange peels for a cozy scent). - **Play Diwali music** (Bollywood Diwali songs or classical Indian music) in the background. ### **5. Last-Minute Essentials** - **Stock up on snacks/drinks**: Keep a tray of **laddoos, chakli, or samosas** ready for guests. - **Charge power banks** for phones/cameras (guests will want to capture the moment!). - **Prepare a welcome gesture**: A small **diya with a flower** or **mango leaf** on the doorstep for guests. ### **6. Day Before Diwali** - **Test all lights/diyas** (replace batteries if needed). - **Set out guest towels/soap** in bathrooms. - **Plan a quick photo spot** (e.g., a decorated corner with diyas and rangoli). ### **Time-Saving Tips:** - **Delegate**: Ask a family member to handle one area (e.g., "You handle the kitchen diyas, I’ll do the living room"). - **Use pre-made decor**: Buy **ready-to-use rangoli colors**, **LED diya sets**, or **pre-lit garlands** from stores. - **Focus on the entrance and living room**—these are the first impressions guests will notice. ### **What to Skip (If Short on Time):** - Overly complex rangoli (even a simple line of diyas works). - Heavy, bulky decor (opt for lightweight items like fairy lights). - Perfuming the entire house (a few incense sticks or a simmer pot suffice). ### **Final Checklist (Night Before):** - [ ] All diyas are lit (or batteries charged). - [ ] Rangoli is set (even if minimal). - [ ] Entrance is welcoming (lights, mango leaves, small diya). - [ ] Snacks/drinks are ready. - [ ] Music is playing (optional but festive!). prediction.raw: This is a nuanced scenario that involves **safety, courtesy, and practicality**, and your friend’s perspective (that you should have moved) has some validity—though your frustration is understandable. Here’s a breakdown of why this situation is **not a clear-cut "right" or "wrong"** but rather a **gray area with reasonable arguments on both sides**: --- ### **Arguments for Your Side (Not Moving Was Justified)** 1. **Traffic Law Violation** - The driver was going the wrong way into the ATM cutout, which is a **de facto one-way zone** (even if not officially marked as such). This is a clear traffic violation, and you weren’t obligated to yield to someone breaking the rules. - If this were a regular road, you’d expect other drivers to follow traffic signs. The same logic applies here—the arrows and ATM placement imply a direction of travel. 2. **Safety Concerns** - Drive-up ATMs are designed for **one-way access** to prevent collisions. The wrong-way driver put themselves (and you) at risk of a side-swipe or rear-end accident, especially since they were struggling with the ATM (distracted by card issues). - You had the right of way, and forcing you to move could have escalated into a dangerous situation (e.g., if they panicked or another car came). 3. **Time Sensitivity** - You were late for class, and their 15-minute delay compounded your stress. While you shouldn’t let minor inconveniences dictate your patience, the **aggressive yelling** (not just a polite request) crossed a line. Their behavior was unreasonable, and your refusal to move was a **calculated stand** against poor etiquette. 4. **Psychological Frustration** - Being yelled at while you’re already annoyed is exhausting. Your refusal to move was a **boundary-setting response** to their hostility, not just stubbornness. This is a common reaction when people feel disrespected. --- ### **Arguments for Your Friend’s Side (You Should Have Moved)** 1. **Practicality of the Situation** - Drive-up ATMs are **not officially one-way zones** in the eyes of the law (unless posted). The arrows are more of a **guideline** than a strict rule. If the ATM is on the left, it’s likely designed for **both sides** to access it (even if it’s less efficient). - The driver may not have realized they were going the wrong way until they were already in the cutout. Backing out smoothly would have been safer than a K-turn (which could have caused a collision). 2. **No Immediate Danger** - There was **no one behind you**, and you weren’t in a rush to the point where you’d cause an accident by refusing to move. The ATM cutout is small, so a quick maneuver wouldn’t have been dangerous. 3. **Courtesy Over Legality** - Even if the driver was technically wrong, **courtesy wins in real-world scenarios**. You could have: - **Gently asked them to back up** (e.g., honking politely or flashing your lights). - **Waited a few seconds** to see if they’d realize their mistake and correct it. - **Moved after they left** (since no one was behind you). - Your **complete refusal** (even after they left) came across as **passive-aggressive**, especially since you didn’t engage with them at all. 4. **The "Butterfly Effect" of Road Rage** - Escalating conflicts on the road often lead to **more dangerous behavior**. Your refusal to move, combined with their yelling, could have triggered a **road rage incident** (e.g., if they tried to force you out). This is why most people yield to avoid confrontation. --- ### **Why This Isn’t a Simple "AITA" Question** - **It’s not a moral failing** to refuse to move in this case—you weren’t doing anything illegal or unsafe. However, **your approach lacked diplomacy**. - **The real issue** wasn’t just the wrong-way driver but **how you handled it**. You could have: - **Ignored them** (since they were wrong and you weren’t in danger). - **Waited patiently** (since they were done in 15 minutes anyway). - **Moved after they left** (to avoid any lingering tension). - **Their behavior was also unreasonable**. Yelling at you for not moving after they were the ones in the wrong is **gaslighting**. But that doesn’t excuse your **complete refusal to engage**. --- ### **How to Handle This Next Time (If It Happens Again)** 1. **Assess the Situation Quickly** - If someone is clearly wrong (e.g., going the wrong way into a one-way zone), **don’t engage**. Just wait it out. - If they’re **not obviously wrong** (e.g., a new driver unsure of the layout), a **polite honk or light tap on the horn** can prompt them to correct their path. 2. **Set Boundaries Without Escalation** - If someone is **yelling or being aggressive**, **don’t respond**. Your silence can be more powerful than confrontation. - If they’re **just confused**, a **calm "Excuse me, you’re going the wrong way"** can work. 3. **Prioritize Safety Over Pride** - If you’re in a situation where **yielding is safer** (e.g., a tight space, heavy traffic), do it—even if you’re annoyed. Road rage is never worth it. 4. **Forgive and Move On** - Both of you were in the wrong in different ways. The driver was **rude and incorrect**, but you were **unnecessarily stubborn**. Neither of you won. --- ### **Final Verdict: <0.5/1> (Neither Fully Right Nor Wrong)** - **You weren’t "wrong"** for refusing to move—you had the right of way and weren’t putting yourself in danger. - **But you weren’t "right"** either, because your **complete refusal to yield** (even after they left) lacked grace. A simple **"Have a good day"** or a nod would have been better than silent defiance. - **The driver was wrong** for going the wrong way and yelling, but **your friend is right** that you could have handled it with more patience. --- ### **Key Takeaway:** Road situations are rarely black-and-white. **Legality, safety, and courtesy** should guide your actions, but **emotions often cloud judgment**. Next time, **assess the risk, stay calm, and prioritize peace over pride**. Would you like advice on how to handle similar situations in the future?
